analysis.one_liner: Exempts livestock manure from Superfund cleanup liability and toxic-release emergency reporting.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or a floor vote and died when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would change two federal laws that deal with hazardous releases. Under the Superfund law (CERCLA), anyone who releases a hazardous substance can be made to pay for cleaning it up; the bill would declare that manure — broadly defined to include animal waste, bedding, process water, and anything in or coming from them — is not a hazardous substance. It would also exempt manure-related releases from the emergency notification rules that require facilities to warn officials and the public when dangerous chemicals are released into the air. Large livestock operations — poultry, hog, and dairy farms with big waste lagoons — would be shielded from cleanup liability and from having to report large ammonia and hydrogen sulfide releases to their neighbors.
analysis.who_benefits: Large livestock operations, especially concentrated animal feeding operations, would gain the most: they would no longer face Superfund cost-recovery liability for manure-linked contamination and would no longer have to make emergency notifications when manure-related gases or wastes are released. Rural communities near these operations would gain nothing from the bill; its protections flow to the operators.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Large poultry, hog, and dairy operations

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends CERCLA to declare that manure is not a 'hazardous substance' or a 'pollutant or contaminant,' removing the threat of Superfund cleanup liability for livestock operators.

It exempts releases associated with manure from the emergency notification requirements of the Superfund Amendments and Reauthorization Act, so operators would not have to report manure-related releases to officials and the public.

It states the exemption would not impose any liability under the Emergency Planning and Community Right-To-Know Act with respect to manure, further limiting operators' reporting and liability exposure.

Supporters could point out that the bill leaves other environmental laws — such as water permitting — untouched, and preserves an existing EPA Air Quality Agreement with animal feeding operations, arguing farms were never the intended target of a toxic-waste cleanup law.

analysis.who_pays: People living near large animal feeding operations would bear the cost: they would lose the emergency notification that warns them and first responders when large quantities of gases like ammonia are released, and if manure-linked contamination required cleanup, the operators would no longer be reachable under Superfund, leaving cleanup costs to taxpayers or affected communities.

drawbacks.text: The emergency-notification exemption means communities near large feeding operations would no longer be warned when manure-associated releases — including ammonia and hydrogen sulfide from waste lagoons — occur, information that matters for people downwind and for first responders.

The definition of 'manure' is broad: it includes bedding, compost, process water, and 'any byproduct, constituent, or substance contained in or originating from' animal waste, which could sweep in contaminants carried in livestock waste and shield operators from Superfund responsibility for them.

An honest supporter would acknowledge that the bill protects operations of every size, including the largest industrial-scale facilities, not just family farms, and that its stated carve-outs for other environmental laws do not restore the two protections it removes — cleanup liability and community notification.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit is real but narrow and concentrated: it removes legal exposure and paperwork for livestock operators. The costs fall on a different group entirely — the rural residents who would lose the right to know about large hazardous releases and who would share cleanup costs if contaminated sites were left without a responsible party. Weighing the two, the bill transfers risk from operators to their neighbors, and its broad definition of manure makes the shield wider than a 'protect family farms' framing suggests.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate introduced the bill and sent it to the Environment and Public Works Committee, which never acted on it, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Pete Domenici introduced the bill on July 18, 2006, with 23 senators joining as original cosponsors.
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works the same day.
The bill accumulated 35 cosponsors — 31 Republicans and 4 Democrats — but the committee never held a markup or vote, and no further action appears in the record before the 109th Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, people living near large livestock operations kept the existing Superfund cleanup tool and the emergency-notification rules; the livestock operators who backed the bill gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Rural residents near large livestock operations

against.what_they_did: Never scheduled committee action on the bill; after its referral on July 18, 2006, the record shows no markup, hearing action, or vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship split sharply by party: 31 of 55 Senate Republicans signed on versus 4 of 44 Senate Democrats, though a handful of Democrats from agricultural states joined.

industries.industry: Large livestock operations (poultry, hog, and dairy concentrated animal feeding operations)
industries.note: The bill would exempt manure — defined broadly to include waste lagoon process water and anything originating from it — from Superfund liability and from emergency release reporting, shifting cleanup and notification burdens away from operators and onto neighbors and taxpayers. Their gain in this bill is precisely the loss of information and cleanup recourse for the communities around them.

Where manure-linked contamination occurs, the loss of Superfund cost recovery from livestock operators could leave cleanup costs with governments and residents. The bill's sponsors did not frame this as a benefit, but it is a foreseeable cost of the exemption.
